items.readme:
# earshot

**Ears for coding agents.**

<!-- launch video -->
[**Watch the 22 s launch film**](https://github.com/Leonxlnx/earshot/releases/tag/v0.1.0) - every sound in it was made
in code by `earshot forge`; no recordings, no music track.

![Frames from the launch film](docs/media/launch_frames.png)

AI coding agents can now write the code that renders a film, a product demo or a game. They still cannot hear what
they made. They cannot tell a premium key press from a cheap one, notice that a hit lands 80 ms after the cut, or
hear that the music swells in the wrong place.

earshot turns sound into evidence an agent can reason about: what a file sounds like in words, how well it fits a
description, the best moment inside a long recording, whether it is a real recording or code-synthesized, a
second-by-second listening transcript of a whole film, an annotated picture of it, and a scorecard against
professional launch films. It runs locally on CPU, as a CLI, a Python API and an MCP server.

With ears, an agent can also **make its own sounds in code** and improve them by listening (`earshot forge`), and
**translate a recording into code** it can vary (`earshot fit`). Both below.

**New in 0.3: sound for code-made films.** A bank of 201 sound effects stored as code that render by id in seconds,
with no models and no network: `earshot sfx` aims a whoosh, hit, click or note at a moment in the picture, and
`earshot kit` renders a whole film's effects with measured sync points ([below](#sound-for-films-bank-sfx-kits)).

```
$ earshot describe enter.ogg
  0.56 s short transient (attack 3 ms, decays in 190 ms). Sounds most like: a single mechanical keyboard key press
  (z +5.4), a soft key release click (z +3.6) ... [clear reading]. peak -0.1 dBFS, brightness 1.5 kHz ...

$ earshot match key.ogg "a deep thocky mechanical keyboard press" --alts "a clicky blue switch keyboard" "a mouse click"
  -> strong (z +3.7; would rank #2 among 322 vocabulary descriptions) ...

$ earshot find keys.ogg "a single mechanical key press" --top 4
  0:03.94-0:04.19 (0.24 s stroke, z +4.1 strong); 0:10.60-0:10.86 ...

$ earshot critique film.mp4
  VERDICT: close - 21 of 23 scored metrics in range ... FIX FIRST: 1. [major] nothing reaches body level until 0:01.01 ...
```

## What it does

| command | what an agent gets |
|---|---|
| `describe FILE` | what it sounds like: calibrated tags (z) with the closest alternative readings, AudioSet labels, measurements |
| `match FILE QUERY [--alts ...]` | how well a description fits: cosine, z among the vocabulary, a verdict (strong / plausible / weak / no match) with held-out evidence |
| `rank QUERY PATHS...` | many candidate files sorted by a description (pick the best download) |
| `find FILE QUERY` | the best moments inside a long recording, as sample trims (start / end seconds) |
| `compare FILE --refs DIR` / `ab A B` | nearest reference recordings and typicality; A/B two sounds or two trims, the differences in words |
| `realness FILE...` | real recording / pro-produced vs code-synthesized, with evidence and per-window scores |
| `timeline FILE [--video V] [--cues C]` | the listening transcript: events (time, level, tag), sections, loudness, beat grid, sync of sound to picture cuts and cue frames |
| `sheet FILE -o out.png` | an annotated PNG (video frames, sections, labelled events, spectrogram, waveform, loudness, sync markers) for agents that read images |
| `critique FILE [--video V]` | a launch-video scorecard against a profile of 7 professional launch films, with timestamped fixes |
| `profile REFS... -o p.json` | build your own reference profile from films you admire |
| `measure FILE` | objective measurements only (no models): LUFS, true peak, LRA, envelope, spectrum, tempo / key |
| `forge RECIPE --refset CAT` | make a sound in code and improve it by listening (see below) |
| `fit FILE -o recipe.py` | translate a recording into a forge recipe module that re-renders it, with knobs and morphs (see below) |
| `sfx render ID -o x.wav` | a sound from the shipped bank of 201, aimed at the picture (`--dur`, `--apex`, `--pitch`) and audited; `sfx list`, `sfx check` (no models) |
| `kit init / render / check` | a film's sound kit: one bank sound per role, rendered into cached takes with measured onset / peak / end (no models) |
| `gallery DIR -o page.html` | one static HTML listening page of forge outputs: players, spectrograms, numbers |
| `llm FILE --yes-upload` | optional audio-LLM critique (Gemini), only with your own key and explicit consent |
| `mcp` | the same tools as an MCP server for Claude Code and other agents |
| `doctor [--load]` | check the install, models, data files and CPU settings |

Every command prints a plain-language summary first; `--json` gives the full result, `--out f.json` saves it. Errors
are one line on stderr (`earshot <command>: error: ...`, exit 1). Each CLI call is a new process and loads the models
(~20-40 s) before it answers (`measure`, `sfx` and `kit` load none): for more than a few calls use the MCP server
(models stay loaded) or one Python script with `from earshot import api`.

What an agent sees when it listens to that film with `earshot sheet` (frames, labelled sound events, spectrogram,
loudness, sync to the beat):

![earshot sheet of the launch film](docs/media/launch_sheet.png)

## Make sounds: earshot forge

Listening makes iteration possible. The agent writes a sound as code: a **recipe** of physical synthesis (modal
resonators, contact excitations, filtered noise, a computed room and a microphone; no recorded audio inside). The
forge renders candidates from the recipe's parameters, and a **critic** built from earshot scores each one:
description match against named confusions, realness, closeness to real reference recordings and measured shape, then
model-free penalties against the references: 1/3-octave tonal balance, the spectro-temporal envelope (a tail that dies
too fast shows here), artifacts (clicks, aliasing, DC / infrasound, harsh resonances, comb ring, cut tails, clipping)
and polish (attack, onset snap, tail smoothness). A cheap model-free **pre-screen** ranks many renders with the same
measurements, so the models only hear the best; an evolutionary **search** keeps the best and mutates them. Then the
agent reads the critic's words ("sounds like: a cork pop, a glass ting", "decay +2.4 outside the refs", "bumpy tail"),
looks at spectrograms next to the references, rewrites the recipe, and runs it again.

```bash
earshot forge --list                             # the recipes (click, impact, keypress, pop, whoosh, ...) + refsets
earshot forge keypress --refs path/to/real/keypresses/ --budget 144 --variants 4 --dir made/keypress
earshot forge whoosh --refset whoosh_fast --budget 96 --dir made/whoosh      # a reference set's 'forge' split
earshot forge whoosh --target "a fast crisp air whoosh" --alts "a wind gust" "a sword swing" \
  --refs path/to/real/whooshes/ --mode real --dir made/whoosh
earshot forge --render keypress --params made/keypress/report.json --seeds 1 2 3 --dir made/again
```

Output (`--dir`): the best diverse sounds as WAVs; `report.md` (what was asked, the search per generation, each pick in
the critic's words, the measured gap to the references); `compare.png` (each pick's spectrogram, envelope and
1/3-octave balance next to its nearest reference); `audition.wav` (made, ref, made, ref ... to listen in pairs);
`report.json` with every candidate's parameters and scores, the same critic's scores of the real references
(leave-one-out) and held-out AudioSet tags. Picks are re-rendered on new seeds (`--robust`, default 3) and must differ
in parameters and in sound. Reference sets (`earshot/forge/refsets.py`) are split by source into a 'forge' side the
search may use and a 'bench' side only the fixed benchmark (`eval/forge/bench.py`) hears. The DSP toolkit for recipes:
`earshot/forge/dsp.py` (sources: modal, noise, air, sweeps, Shepard risers, sub drops, bells, FM; layering) and
`earshot/forge/fx.py` (reverb, saturation, transient shaping, limiter, EQ match, Doppler, filters, glitch, granular).
In Python: `from earshot.forge import forge`.

**forge v2 (0.2.0).** Recipes come as families of named characters: 34 motion-design categories (whooshes, swishes,
swipes, risers, downlifters, zips, impacts, sub drops, logo stings, clicks, taps, toggles, hover ticks, pops,
notification dings, shimmers, glitches, key presses), 16 of them modelled on the designed effects of professional
launch films ([docs/motion-sfx-study.md](docs/motion-sfx-study.md)), 4-6 variants each. A fixed benchmark scores them
against held-out recordings the forge never heard. Against v1 on it: variants are no longer near copies (CLAP cosine
between variants 0.89-0.97 -> 0.71-0.85 in the five categories v1 had; real sets 0.52-0.77), tails that died too fast
now reach the real length (click t40 0.56 -> 1.44 x the bench median, fast whoosh 0.51 -> 0.88), and the tonal
balance is closer in 3 of those 5 (key press 8.2 -> 7.4 dB, fast whoosh 8.6 -> 6.2, impact 6.7 -> 4.4). Across all
34, the made balance is at least as close to the held-out recordings as a second set of real recordings in 18 of the
21 categories that have a number, and every final re-renders from its `report.json` (`earshot forge --check`). The
model checks that v1 had saturated fell. A clean blind-test kit for the v2 sounds is `eval/forge/blind_v2.py`; no v2
score is published yet (docs/SFX.md says the same), so the blind test below is the v1 one. What changed, every number, and what is still weak: [docs/FORGE_V2.md](docs/FORGE_V2.md).

The reference recordings are licensed and not in this repo, so `--refset` needs a local registry: bring your own refs
with `--refs DIR`, or lay them out as described in `earshot/forge/refsets.py`. Without refs the critic runs in
designed mode (realness reported, not required). The CLI defaults changed in 0.2.0 (pre-screen, seed bank, robust
re-renders, the recipe's reference set); the Python `forge()` defaults still reproduce v1. See
[CHANGELOG.md](CHANGELOG.md).

**Blind test (v1 recipes).** A key press, a UI click, a pop, a fast whoosh and an impact were made from scratch in
code and played blind next to real recordings of the same kind of sound. The author picked the made one correctly **8 times out
of 15**: a coin flip. Only the made impact was spotted (its tail dies too fast). One listener and 15 trials is a small
test, not a proof; it says the made sounds are no longer easy to tell from real ones.

**Honest limits (Goodhart).** The search optimises earshot's own models, and those can be pleased without the sound
getting better. After a search the made sounds pass every model check, held-out ones included, so the model checks
stop telling made from real; the 1/3-octave measurement still can. The realness model is easy to fool (a modal
resonator plus a room and a noise floor reads "real"). Judge a made sound by the model-free measurements,
spectrograms next to the references, robust re-renders, and a human blind test.

## earshot fit: audio to code

`earshot fit` translates a recording into code by analysis by synthesis. It fits a small synthesis model with readable
parameters (ringing modes, tracked partials, a time-varying noise gesture, or a layered hybrid of them) until its
render matches the recording, then writes the model as a forge recipe module whose `render()` makes the sound. The
module stores the structure of the sound, not its samples, so it can make new takes, variations (size, damping,
pitch, brightness, decay, ...) and morphs between two recordings.

```bash
earshot fit click.wav -o made/click_fit.py --report    # recipe + its render + side-by-side spectrogram + metrics
python made/click_fit.py 3 take3.wav                   # the module renders on its own (seed 3)
earshot fit --morph a.wav b.wav --amount 0.5 -o made/ab_morph.py
earshot fit --forge made/click_fit.py --budget 96 --dir made/click_variations   # critic-searched variations
```

Measured on 12 real recordings (2 each of click, key press, pop, impact, fast whoosh, notification): median CLAP
cosine 0.945 between each recording and the render of its generated code (minimum 0.881), and the same top
`earshot describe` tag in 10 of 12. In our 12-trial blind test (recording vs render, loudness-matched, random order)
the listener could not tell which clip was the recording. One listener is a small test, not a proof. The renders are
close, not identical: onsets, tone balance and noise texture still differ measurably; the selection weights were set
on the same 12 recordings; risers, zips and long designed sounds are untested. A fit is a derivative of its recording,
so keep the source's licence with the recipe. Limits: [docs/FIT.md](docs/FIT.md#limits-honest).

## Sound for films: bank, sfx, kits

The forge's delivered sounds ship as a bank that renders by id, with no models and no network: 183 forge v2 finals
(34 categories), each stored as its render block and re-rendering its delivered WAV to one 24-bit step, three tuned
kalimba voices, and 15 sounds fitted from CC0 recordings (clicks, a tick, pops, touches, keys, a snap, a bell, a
whoosh; credits in [docs/CREDITS_FIT.md](docs/CREDITS_FIT.md)). A film pipeline renders from it in seconds; searching
and fitting new sounds stay offline steps.

```bash
earshot sfx list --kind whoosh                                      # ids, lengths, peak times, cue kinds, knobs
earshot sfx render whoosh_fast/crisp -o w.wav --dur 0.8 --apex 0.32  # a new take aimed at a move (--seed N)
earshot sfx render pluck/kalimba -o e5.wav --pitch E5                # tuned through the recipe's own f0
earshot sfx check w.wav                                              # clicks, cut tails, clipping, ring, rising glides
earshot kit init --preset calm -o audio/kit.json                     # calm | crisp | minimal
earshot kit render audio/kit.json --out audio/kit                    # takes + kit.lock.json (measured onset / peak / end)
```

- **Knobs** edit each recipe's own parameters, never resample: `dur` lands exactly, `apex` puts a whoosh's loudest
  moment within 5 ms of the target (measured within 2.5 ms), `pitch` takes a note name or Hz (pluck E5, a bell G5, a
  sub drop G1 measure 0 cents off); noise sounds refuse a pitch and say why.
- **The audit** (`earshot sfx check`, run on every render) is measurement only: clicks, cut tails, clipping, DC, comb
  ring, a re-rising tail, a tonal pitch that climbs more than 4 semitones (the rising "synth whip"), and for hits,
  stacked attacks or a build before the hit. 185 of the 201 sounds are clean; the presets use none of the others.
- **Kits** name one sound per role (tick, hit, whoosh.short, key, bell, text ...). `kit render` writes deterministic,
  cached takes and a lock with each take's measured sync points; a take that fails the audit is re-rolled on a new
  seed. The three presets sound every role but riser, swell and suck, use one clean hit for the lockup, and use the
  fitted recordings for clicks, ticks, keys, touches and the snap where they measure closer to the role than the
  forge member (earshot match and realness).
- **Python and MCP**: `from earshot.forge import bank; y, meta = bank.render('pro_sub_drop/ref', pitch='G1')`;
  `earshot.api.sfx_render / kit_render`; MCP tools `sfx_list`, `sfx_render`, `kit_render`.

Full reference (every knob, the audit, the kit and lock formats, the presets role by role, fit entries from
public-domain recordings, measured cost): [docs/SFX.md](docs/SFX.md). How cinetic uses it:
[docs/INTEGRATION.md](docs/INTEGRATION.md#cinetic-uses-earshot).

## Gallery

`earshot gallery` turns forge outputs into one static HTML page for people with ears: no server, no network, no
external scripts, inline CSS. One card per category, grouped by family (whooshes, sweeps, impacts, UI, tonal,
digital); per sound a player, a spectrogram thumbnail (log frequency, one time span per card so lengths compare),
duration, peak and momentary-max LUFS, the critic's total / pass, and the recipe parameters of every variant in a
collapsible table. The repo holds no audio, so point it at your own forge runs (`out/forge_v2` below is one folder
per category).

```bash
earshot gallery out/forge_v2 -o out/gallery/gallery.html                  # <category>/final/*.wav (+ report.json)
earshot gallery out/forge_v2 -o g.html --results eval/forge/results_v2r6.json   # + held-out benchmark numbers
earshot gallery out/forge_v2 -o g.html --refs forge                        # + A/B row: each sound's nearest forge ref
earshot gallery --compare "r2:out/forge_v2/*/final_r2" "r3:out/forge_v2/*/final" -o compare.html \
  --results r2:eval/forge/results_v2r2.json                                # before / after, variant under variant
earshot gallery out/forge_v2 -o portable.html --embed                      # audio (FLAC) + images inside the file
earshot gallery out/forge_v2 -o share.html --embed-compressed              # one small file: MP3 previews, plays anywhere
earshot gallery --compare "v1:old/*/final" "v2:out/forge_v2/*/final" --alias keypress=typing_key -o v1_v2.html
```

Audio is referenced by relative path (or embedded with `--embed`); thumbnails go to `<page>_files/` next to the page
and are cached by content. `--embed-compressed` makes one self-contained page to send or open on a phone: each sound
encoded by ffmpeg (MP3 192 kbps by default; `--embed-codec opus` or `vorbis` for Ogg, `--kbps` for the rate), JPEG
thumbnails, no links to local files; 183 sounds come to about 9 MB. The numbers on it are still measured on the WAVs.
`--alias OLD=NEW` puts a folder under another category's card (an older recipe's `keypress` under `typing_key`).
A "match loudness" switch (on by default) turns louder players down so a riser does not blast after a click; it
changes the player volume only, never the files. Benchmark numbers are shown only for files the benchmark actually
measured: a file newer than the results JSON, or with another length / peak, gets none (renamed files are matched by
length and peak, and the page lists every such case). In `--compare`, files identical to an earlier version are marked
`= r2`. Bench references never go on a page: `--refs bench` is refused, every reference passes `refsets.held_out()`,
and only the benchmark's numbers are shown, never its file names. Forge references are licensed recordings: keep a
page that plays them private. In Python: `from earshot.gallery import gallery`.

## Install

Python 3.10+ and ffmpeg / ffprobe on PATH. CPU only; no GPU is used.

```bash
git clone https://github.com/Leonxlnx/earshot && cd earshot
python -m venv .venv
.venv/bin/python -m pip install torch --index-url https://download.pytorch.org/whl/cpu   # Windows: .venv/Scripts/python
.venv/bin/python -m pip install -e ".[mcp,llm,dev]"
.venv/bin/python -m earshot doctor --load
```

The first model use downloads two open models (~1.1 GB) into `.cache/hf` inside the repo (or `EARSHOT_HOME`), each at
a pinned revision with safetensors weights: CLAP `laion/larger_clap_general` @ `16c8cc3` (text-audio embeddings; the
Hub's safetensors conversion of its main revision) and the AudioSet tagger `MIT/ast-finetuned-audioset-10-10-0.4593`
@ `f826b80`. `earshot doctor --fetch` downloads them up front. After that earshot loads them from that cache only and
never contacts the Hub; a damaged cache is an error that names the folder, not a silent new download.

Offline: `EARSHOT_OFFLINE=1`, `HF_HUB_OFFLINE=1` and `TRANSFORMERS_OFFLINE=1` all mean the same to earshot: it never
downloads, and a model missing from the cache is an error that says so. earshot never sets or clears these variables.

A cache made before 0.2.1 holds CLAP's main revision `ada0c23`, whose only weights are a pickle (`pytorch_model.bin`,
the same tensors). earshot still loads it from the cache (torch `weights_only`), never downloads it, and `earshot
doctor` says so; `earshot doctor --fetch` downloads the pinned safetensors (776 MB), used from then on.

Settings (environment variables): `EARSHOT_THREADS` (torch CPU threads, default min(4, cores/2)), `EARSHOT_HOME`
(cache root), `EARSHOT_PRECISION` (`bf16` by default, used only on CPUs with native bf16 such as AVX512-BF16 / AMX,
fp32 everywhere else; `fp32` forces fp32), `EARSHOT_OFFLINE=1` (above), `EARSHOT_CLAP` / `EARSHOT_AST` (another
Hub model id, or a local model folder with `config.json` and `model.safetensors`, which loads from disk as it is with
no network and is never downloaded into) and `EARSHOT_CLAP_REVISION` / `EARSHOT_AST_REVISION` (another Hub revision;
safetensors weights only). A custom Hub model downloads its top-level config, tokenizer and safetensors files by name,
never a repo's subfolders or weight variants.
`earshot doctor` reports the revisions and what the cache holds; `--load` also what loads (revision, weights,
precision).

### MCP server for Claude Code

```bash
claude mcp add earshot --scope user -e EARSHOT_THREADS=3 -- /path/to/earshot/.venv/bin/python -m earshot mcp
```

Or in any client's `.mcp.json`:

```json
{"mcpServers": {"earshot": {"command": "/path/to/earshot/.venv/bin/python", "args": ["-m", "earshot", "mcp"],
  "env": {"EARSHOT_THREADS": "3"}}}}
```

Models load on the first call and stay warm. On a slow machine start Claude Code with `MCP_TIMEOUT=60000`. The
optional `llm_critique` tool reads `GEMINI_API_KEY` from the environment; never write a literal key into a file.

### Python

```python
import earshot
earshot.describe('whoosh.wav')
earshot.find('typing.ogg', 'a single isolated key press')
earshot.timeline('soundtrack.wav', video='film.mp4')
from earshot import api   # everything in one namespace: api.rank, api.critique, api.realness_many, ...
```

## Agent skills

Two skills ship in `skills/`. Copy or symlink them into `~/.claude/skills/` (or a project's `.claude/skills/`).

- **`skills/earshot`**: how an agent should listen with earshot: which command answers which question, how to read
  the verdicts, when not to trust them.
- **`skills/real-sound`**: a full process for premium, realistic soundtracks for code-made films from real licensed
  recordings: sourcing with licence checks, a music edit, a JSON sound design, a deterministic mixer, measured QA, a
  multi-lens critique, mastering, credits and mux. earshot chooses, trims and verifies the sounds.

## How good is it?

Every number below comes with the command that measured it in [docs/VALIDATION.md](docs/VALIDATION.md). What
earshot cannot judge is in [docs/LIMITS.md](docs/LIMITS.md).

- **Matching descriptions** (a held-out library of 125 real recordings, nothing tuned on it): in a library search a
  "strong" verdict is the right kind of sound 98% of the time and the exact variant 61% of the time.
- **Finding the moment**: on a recording of 17 single key presses the found trims land on real key presses; in a
  300 s scene every planted event is found as a tight trim.
- **Real vs code-synthesized**: held-out ROC-AUC 0.92 with whole sound families held out. Firm verdicts call 6.7% of
  real clips synthesized and 5.5% of synthesized clips real; a fifth of clips get "uncertain".
- **Listening through a soundtrack**: 93% of the sound effects placed in a 60 s film mix are detected as events (89%
  of the quiet ones under music). A 60-90 s film takes about 1.5 minutes on a laptop CPU.
- **Launch scorecard**: each reference film critiqued against the other six falls in range on 86% of the metrics
  (the no-overfit baseline is about 71%; some rules changed after the first run, so it is not a blind test).

## Limits

earshot hears through two open models and a set of measurements. Trustworthy: loudness, timing and sync to picture,
"is this the kind of sound I asked for" on single exposed sounds, picking among candidates, obvious code-synthesized
sources. Hints only: tags of events inside a busy mix, music genre and mood. It cannot judge taste or emotion,
provenance or licences, speech content, or anything above 14 kHz from the models. The launch scorecard describes the
style of the 7 films behind it, not every good film. Details in [docs/LIMITS.md](docs/LIMITS.md).

## Repo map

```
earshot/            the package: CLI, Python API, MCP server, CPU model wrappers
  forge/            make sounds in code: DSP building blocks, critic, model-free tone checks, search, recipes/
    fit/            recording -> code: modal / sines / spectral fitters, quality metrics, recipe codegen
    bank/, kits/    the sound bank (render blocks + fingerprints, no audio) and the kit presets: earshot sfx / kit
  gallery.py        the static listening page
  data/             vocabulary + calibration stats, realness model weights, launch profile (numbers only, no media)
skills/earshot/     agent skill: how to listen with earshot
skills/real-sound/  agent skill: real-recordings soundtracks (scripts, templates, prompts, references)
docs/               VALIDATION, LIMITS, FORGE_V2, FIT, SFX, the motion-SFX study, launch-video playbook, design notes
eval/               evaluation scripts and results per area (see eval/README.md)
tests/              pytest (fast by default; --slow loads the models)
```

No audio or video is stored in this repo. The evaluation data (licensed recordings and third-party films) is not
redistributed; only derived numbers are committed.

## Licence

MIT for the code (see [LICENSE](LICENSE)). The models are downloaded from their authors under their own licences:
CLAP (`laion/larger_clap_general`) Apache-2.0, AST (`MIT/ast-finetuned-audioset-10-10-0.4593`) BSD-3-Clause.
`skills/real-sound/scripts/master.py` is vendored from the Cinetic skill by the same author.

items.description: Overdrive, a PS5 homebrew game store with 1,800+ games.
items.readme:
English · Русский

Your PS5 game store.
Back from the dead, rebuilt from its own binary, with every line of source in the open.

Install · Features · Updates · Troubleshooting · Build it yourself

> [!NOTE] > The original Overdrive project has been shut down so I decompiled the last released build, > recovered the complete source and rebuilt it.

## Features - **1,800+ games** to discover, with **Top rated**, **New releases** and a featured spotlight - **Browse the whole library** with filters, sorting, scores and download sizes at a glance - **Downloads straight to the console**, to internal storage or any USB drive, with live speed and storage stats - **Favorites**, **search** with an on-screen keyboard, and a **Files** page to see and clean up what's on your drives - **13 languages**: English, Deutsch, Español, Français, Português (Brasil), Русский, Bahasa Indonesia, 日本語, 简体中文, العربية, اردو, हिन्दी, বাংলা - **Updates itself**: a new version installs from the console, no PC needed - Made for the controller: L1 R1 to switch sections, ✕ to select, ○ to go back ## Install in four steps

### Before you start You need a **jailbroken PS5** running two payloads: **[ShadowMount+](https://github.com/drakmor/ShadowMountPlus)**, which installs `.exfat` images by itself, and **[kstuff](https://github.com/EchoStretch/kstuff-lite/releases)**. If ShadowMount+ shows its notification when the console starts, you are ready. You also need a **USB drive** and a **PC**.

**Download `Overdrive.exfat`** with the button above, or from the [latest release](https://github.com/MyLuxy/overdrive/releases/latest). It is the only file you need. Leave it as it is: don't unzip it and don't change the `.exfat` at the end of its name.
**Copy it onto a USB drive, inside a folder called `homebrew`.** Plug the drive into your PC, create a new folder named exactly `homebrew` (all lowercase) at the top level of the drive, and copy `Overdrive.exfat` into it: ```text USB drive └── homebrew └── Overdrive.exfat ``` The drive must be formatted as **exFAT**, which is how most drives come and what the PS5 reads.
**Plug the drive into the PS5.** ShadowMount+ checks for new files every few seconds: it finds Overdrive, mounts it and installs it, and a notification tells you when it's done. There is nothing to click.
**Open Overdrive from the home screen.** Look for this icon. Enjoy!
You can also use **any FTP client** to move the file onto the console's internal storage instead, again inside a `homebrew` folder: `/data/homebrew/Overdrive.exfat`. ## Updates You only install Overdrive by hand once. When a new version comes out, the app tells you by itself a few seconds after it opens: 1. A window shows the new version and what changed. Press **Install**. 2. Overdrive downloads the update, checks it and puts it in place of the old one. 3. When it's done, the app **closes itself**. Open it again and you are on the new version. The update needs about **600 MB free** on the drive that holds Overdrive. `update.zip` in each release is the package the app downloads for this; you never need it yourself. ## Support the project Overdrive is free and open source. If you enjoy it, sponsoring helps me keep it updated.

## Troubleshooting
Overdrive doesn't appear on the home screen
- Make sure **ShadowMount+ is running**: it shows a notification when it starts. - Check the folder: it must be called exactly `homebrew` and sit at the **top level** of the drive, not inside another folder. - Check the file still ends in **`.exfat`**. Some PCs hide extensions: a file renamed to `Overdrive.exfat.zip` or unzipped into a folder won't be found. - Give it a minute: ShadowMount+ waits until the file has finished copying before it installs it.
After an update, the app still shows the old version
The new version is installed but the console still has the old one loaded. **Restart the console** and open Overdrive again; the app tells you this itself if it happens twice in a row.
The update says there isn't enough space
The update is downloaded next to the installed app, so the drive holding Overdrive needs about 600 MB free. Free some space on that drive and press **Retry**. Nothing has been changed yet when this happens.
The update says it couldn't replace the app
Install it by hand: download `Overdrive.exfat` from the [latest release](https://github.com/MyLuxy/overdrive/releases/latest), close Overdrive, and copy the new file over the old one in the `homebrew` folder.
How do I remove Overdrive?
Delete `Overdrive.exfat` from the `homebrew` folder first, then delete its icon from the home screen. In the other order ShadowMount+ finds the file again and puts the icon back.
## Build it yourself
What's in this repository
| Path | What it is | | --- | --- | | `app/` | The application: JSX sources, state, assets, catalog data, and `app.json` (title id `PPSA99058`, version, capabilities) | | `ps5-react/` | The framework it runs on, vendored from [half144/ps5-react](https://github.com/half144/ps5-react) | | `packaging/make-exfat.sh` | Builds the exFAT image ShadowMount+ installs | | `.github/workflows/build.yml` | The build |
How the source was recovered
Overdrive is a React app running on [ps5-react](https://github.com/half144/ps5-react), and its whole JavaScript bundle sits in plain text inside `eboot.bin`. A bundler merges every module into one scope, so imports between modules turn into bare names; since each top-level name stays unique, the module that declares a name can be worked out again. That split the bundle back into its 137 original modules with their real `import`/`export` lines, checked against the original bundle until every import edge matched. What a bundler throws away could not come back: most comments, the JSX syntax (it reads as `jsx(View, {…})` calls), and `const`/`let` (now `var`). None of that changes how the app behaves.
Developing
Everything runs from the repository root through npm. Once after cloning, `npm run setup` (`packaging/setup.sh`) installs every dependency: on Linux the apt packages for the desktop preview, the PS5 build and the tests (it asks for `sudo` once), on macOS the Homebrew formulae; then Pillow and the framework's npm packages. Read the script first if you'd rather install them yourself. ```sh git clone https://github.com/MyLuxy/overdrive.git cd overdrive npm run setup # once; asks for sudo on Linux npm run dev # the app in a window on your PC, rebuilt on every save under app/ ``` | Command | What it does | | --- | --- | | `npm run setup` | Installs every dependency, once after cloning | | `npm run dev` | Opens the app in the desktop preview and rebuilds it on every save (state resets on restart) | | `npm run preview` | Opens the desktop preview once, without watching | | `npm test` | The framework's checks; needed after changes under `ps5-react/`, not for `app/` only | | `npm run build` | The PS5 app, then `Overdrive.exfat` and `update.zip` (see Building) | | `npm run build:app` | The PS5 app only, in `ps5-react/dist/PPSA99058` | The preview is the console's UI on your PC, so it takes a controller or the keyboard, and a mouse as a developer's shortcut. The first `npm run dev` downloads and compiles the framework's pinned dependencies, which takes a while; later starts are quick. | Action | Keyboard | Mouse | PS5 | | --- | --- | --- | --- | | Move focus | Arrow keys | Wheel (up/down) | D-pad | | Select | Enter or Space | Left click on the element | ✕ | | Back | Backspace | Right click | ○ | | Sections | Q / E | — | L1 / R1 | | Favorite | F | — | □ | | Quit the preview | Escape | — | PS button | The app's code is under `app/` (see "What's in this repository"); a change there needs no rebuild of the framework. Keep new user-facing strings in every file of `app/i18n/locales/`. On Linux the preview is compiled with clang (`CC=clang CXX=clang++`, set by the npm scripts), since GCC stops on a bounds warning in `archive_preflight.cpp`. Linux support for the preview is this fork's addition; upstream ps5-react supports macOS only.
Building
Builds run on `ubuntu-24.04` with clang 18, only from **Run workflow**: a push builds nothing. Each run puts `Overdrive.exfat` and `update.zip` in a draft release named after `app/version.js`, which only maintainers can see. The same build locally, from the repository root, after `npm run setup` (see Developing): ```sh npm run build # the app, then Overdrive.exfat and update.zip here npm run build:app # the app only, in ps5-react/dist/PPSA99058 ``` `packaging/build.sh` behind them finds LLVM 18 where apt or Homebrew put it (set `LLVM=` otherwise), builds through `ps5-react/tools/build_ps5.py`, then runs `packaging/make-exfat.sh` under `sudo`, since the image is mounted to be filled. The build downloads its pinned dependencies into `ps5-react/.deps` and writes the app folder, a `.zip` and a `.receipt.json` into `ps5-react/dist`. It verifies the result itself (`tools/verify.py`), so a green build means the payload structure and signatures check out. The image is a plain exFAT volume whose root is the app folder, with 64 KiB clusters and the label `OVERDRIVE`. To release a new version, raise the version in `app/version.js` and `app/app.json`, run the workflow, test the draft's image on a console, then publish the draft: that creates its tag, and installed apps offer exactly the tested files on their next start.
Fixes over upstream ps5-react
Two fixes in the vendored framework, both in the build tooling and both reported by a Linux build: - `ps5-react/tools/common.py` read the `git apply --summary` line with a fixed space count, which glued the file mode onto the path (`100644 `) and made every fresh dependency checkout fail on the first patch that creates a file. It now splits on whitespace. - `ps5-react/tools/build_ps5.py` opened the pinned LLVM package's `data.tar.zst` with `tarfile`, which reads zstd only from Python 3.14 while the documented minimum is 3.12. It now falls back to the `zstd` command. Nothing else in the framework is changed.
## Credits - **[MyLuxy](https://github.com/MyLuxy)**, who decompiled Overdrive, recovered its source and rebuilt it. - **[ps5-react](https://github.com/half144/ps5-react)**, the framework it runs on. - **[ShadowMount+](https://github.com/drakmor/ShadowMountPlus)** by drakmor, which installs it. `ps5-react/` is GPL-3.0-or-later and carries its own `LICENSE`, `LICENSE-ATTRIBUTION` and `NOTICE`. Every dependency notice is copied into `notices/` inside the built app, and `ps5-react/docs/DEPENDENCIES.md` lists them with their sources. Overdrive is an unofficial homebrew project and is not affiliated with or endorsed by Sony Interactive Entertainment. PlayStation and PS5 are trademarks of Sony Interactive Entertainment.

# mcp-for-blender-pro

### Your Blender scene. Your AI models. One creative workspace.

**An AI assistant for Blender that can inspect your scene, build objects, edit materials, find assets and carry out multi-step workflows—with a visual chat workspace and a built-in Model Context Protocol (MCP) server.**

![Blender 4.2+](https://img.shields.io/badge/Blender-4.2%2B-E87D0D?logo=blender&logoColor=white)
![Release 1.0.0](https://img.shields.io/badge/release-1.0.0-98D85B)
![Windows x64](https://img.shields.io/badge/download-Windows_x64-357EC7)
![MIT](https://img.shields.io/badge/license-MIT-blue)

[Download](../../releases/latest) · [Getting started](docs/QUICKSTART.md) · [Connections and agents](docs/CONNECTIONS.md)

![AI chat workspace with a live Blender scene preview](docs/images/studio.png)

## Turn a creative brief into scene operations

Start with an idea. Ask the assistant to inspect your scene, create a product-display layout, arrange objects, assign materials or prepare an export. Follow its actions in the conversation and inspect the result in the viewport preview. Keep working in Blender throughout the process.

**mcp-for-blender-pro brings conversation, scene tools, model choice and agent workflows together.** It is designed for artists who want faster iteration, technical artists who automate repetitive work, and developers connecting AI tools to Blender.

## Why choose mcp-for-blender-pro?

| Capability | What it gives you |
|---|---|
| **Blender-aware assistance** | Scene and object inspection gives the assistant context before it acts. |
| **A visual Studio workspace** | Chat, scene objects, viewport snapshots, approvals and a task board in a companion window. |
| **Your choice of AI** | Connect supported cloud providers, local Ollama models or compatible custom endpoints. |
| **Saved connections** | Keep work and personal connections separate, including multiple keys for the same provider. |
| **One assistant or a team** | Use a single model for quick changes, or managers, workers and reviewers for structured tasks. |
| **Built-in MCP server** | Connect OpenCode and other clients supporting authenticated Streamable HTTP MCP. |
| **21 scene tools** | Create, inspect, edit, capture, search assets, consult Blender APIs and export scenes. |
| **Multilingual menus** | Choose English, German, French, Spanish or Chinese for the main interface. |

## From a quick edit to an agent team

Use **Single assistant** for direct, conversational work. For larger tasks, configure a **Team chain** with individual responsibilities, instructions and models.

- **Manager:** breaks the request into assignments and acceptance criteria.
- **Workers:** perform the assigned scene operations.
- **Reviewers:** inspect results and approve work or return specific findings.

Tasks run sequentially so scene edits stay ordered. A blocked task gets one correction attempt; a second failed review stops the workflow. The task board exposes assignments, attempts and review findings as work progresses.

![Agent roles and model configuration](docs/images/studio-team.png)

## Connect the models that fit your work

Supported connections include **OpenAI, Anthropic Claude, Google Gemini, OpenRouter, OpenCode Zen, Ollama and custom APIs**. Load the available model catalog and select a model directly in Blender or Studio.

Custom endpoints support OpenAI Chat Completions, Anthropic Messages and Ollama protocols. Choose models with tool-calling support; image-capable models can also interpret viewport screenshots. OpenCode-only free models are available through the OpenCode client.

![Provider, saved connection and model selection](docs/images/studio-settings.png)

## Install and create

1. Download **`mcp-for-blender-pro.zip`** from [Releases](../../releases/latest).
2. In Blender, open **Edit → Preferences → Get Extensions → menu → Install from Disk**.
3. Select the ZIP, enable **mcp-for-blender-pro**, then open **3D Viewport → N → MCP Pro**.
4. Choose a provider, add your connection details and select a model.
5. Send a message in Blender or click **Open Studio Window**.

The release bundle targets **Windows x64 with Blender 4.2 or later**. Keep Blender open while using Studio or an external client.

### Try these prompts

> Inspect this scene and explain its object structure before making any changes.

> Create a simple product-display scene with a pedestal, a camera and three lights. Give the pedestal a matte blue material.

> Duplicate the selected object into a neatly spaced row of five and show the viewport.

> Find an appropriate Poly Haven asset for this scene and ask before importing it.

## Blender automation through MCP

Launch **OpenCode Portable** from the sidebar to work through OpenCode with the Blender connection configured for you. OpenCode manages its own provider sign-in and model selection. Other compatible MCP clients can connect to the authenticated local endpoint described in the [connection guide](docs/CONNECTIONS.md).

| Tool group | Included tools |
|---|---|
| Scene inspection | `get_scene_info`, `list_objects`, `get_object_info` |
| Object creation | `add_cube`, `add_sphere`, `add_cylinder`, `add_plane`, `add_light`, `add_camera` |
| Editing | `move_object`, `duplicate_object`, `delete_object`, `parent_objects`, `set_material` |
| Visual feedback and scripting | `viewport_screenshot`, `execute_code` |
| Blender API and export | `bpy_api_lookup`, `describe_node_type`, `export_scene` |
| Asset workflows | `search_assets`, `import_asset` |

Asset integrations include **Poly Haven, Sketchfab and Poly Pizza**. Configure service keys where required and follow the licenses of the assets you use.

## Stay in control of your scene

Built-in chat supports operation approvals, cancellation after the current step and named undo steps for mutations. Python tool validation helps catch disallowed operations; it is not a security sandbox. External MCP clients manage their own approval policies.

Connection credentials are stored in your user settings. Chat history lasts for the current session. Studio runs locally and authenticates requests to Blender.

## Keywords

Hy Memory

Production-grade dual-system cognitive memory for LLM agents.

English | [中文](README.zh.md) **[Hy Memory](https://memory.hunyuan.tencent.com/)** ([Official Website](https://memory.hunyuan.tencent.com/)) is a production-grade dual-system cognitive memory engine and Python SDK (`hy-memory`) for self-evolving LLM agents, providing specialized memory pipelines across three task scenes: hierarchical long-term cognitive memory for **Chat**, two-layer fact and reusable-experience memory for **Working**, and version-evolution diff-chain tracking for **Coding**. Built on top of Hy Memory, **[MemHub](memhub/README.md)** is a local-first desktop and CLI product that unifies conversation history and coding traces from user-authorized AI applications (such as Claude Code, Cursor, Codex, OpenCode, and Qwen Code) into a single managed runtime and local data directory, enabling governed cross-application memory recall.

MemHub Demo Video

--- ## Latest News * *[new]* 🔥🔥🔥 **[2026-10]**: 📦 **Released [MemHub v1.0.4](https://github.com/Tencent-Hunyuan/Hy-Memory/releases/tag/v1.0.4)** and **[memhub-cli 1.0.5](https://www.npmjs.com/package/memhub-cli/v/1.0.5)**, with a signed macOS desktop app and verified macOS/Linux Runtimes! * *[new]* 🔥🔥 **[2026-09]**: 📊 **Released** **[CMB: A Coding Memory Benchmark for Long-Horizon and Interleaved Coding Agents](docs/papers/CMB_A_Coding_Memory_Benchmark_for_Long_Horizon_and_Interleaved_Coding_Agents.pdf)** (submitted to **ICLR 2027**). * *[new]* 🔥🔥 **[2026-08]**: 🎉 **Accepted** at **EMNLP 2026**: **[Memory Beyond Recall: A Dual-Process Cognitive Memory System for Self-Evolving LLM Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.09483)**! * 🔥 **[2026-05]**: 🌟 **Initial Release** Released **[Hy Memory 1.0](https://mp.weixin.qq.com/s/dH5PGpxqArFZkSq3-QxWYA)**, our first-generation dual-system cognitive memory framework for self-evolving LLM agents. --- ## Papers Welcome to the **Hy Memory Research Family**, covering cognitive chat memory, long-horizon coding memory, and RL-trained memory writing models: > [**Memory Beyond Recall: A Dual-Process Cognitive Memory System for Self-Evolving LLM Agents**](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.09483) *(Accepted at **EMNLP 2026**)* > **TL;DR:** Proposes the dual-process (System 1 + System 2) cognitive memory architecture for **Chat**, organizing personal memory into an 8-layer hierarchy (raw dialogues, atomic facts, summaries, schemas, and prospective intentions) with conflict reconciliation and cross-domain schema induction. > 📄 Paper: https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.09483 > [**CMB: A Coding Memory Benchmark for Long-Horizon and Interleaved Coding Agents**](docs/papers/CMB_A_Coding_Memory_Benchmark_for_Long_Horizon_and_Interleaved_Coding_Agents.pdf) *(Submitted to **ICLR 2027**)* > **TL;DR:** Introduces a benchmark and two-layer + version-evolution diff-chain memory method for long-horizon **Coding** agents, preserving both reusable engineering experiences and exact code revision trajectories across interleaved tasks. > 📄 Paper: [docs/papers/CMB_A_Coding_Memory_Benchmark_for_Long_Horizon_and_Interleaved_Coding_Agents.pdf](docs/papers/CMB_A_Coding_Memory_Benchmark_for_Long_Horizon_and_Interleaved_Coding_Agents.pdf) > [**Hy-Memory-30B-A3B: Attributed Reinforcement Learning for Long-Term Memory Writing**](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.22196) *(Open Model Technical Report)* > **TL;DR:** Trains a 30B-A3B MoE model via attributed reinforcement learning specifically for high-precision long-term memory extraction and conflict reconciliation. > 📄 Paper: https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.22196 · Model: https://huggingface.co/tencent/Hy-Memory-30B-A3B --- ## Quick Start ### 1. Installation ```bash pip install hy-memory==2.0.3 # core (includes ChromaDB and Kuzu) pip install "hy-memory[qdrant]==2.0.3" # + Qdrant pip install "hy-memory[faiss]==2.0.3" # + FAISS pip install "hy-memory[graph]==2.0.3" # + Neo4j pip install "hy-memory[mysql]==2.0.3" # + MySQL cache pip install "hy-memory[rerank]==2.0.3" # + local multilingual cross-encoder rerank pip install "hy-memory[all]==2.0.3" # everything ``` ### 2. Configuration Only an LLM and an embedding endpoint are needed; any OpenAI-compatible service works: ```bash export MEMORY_LLM_API_KEY="sk-your-key" export MEMORY_LLM_BASE_URL="https://api.deepseek.com" export MEMORY_LLM_MODEL="deepseek-chat" export MEMORY_EMBEDDER_API_KEY="sk-your-key" export MEMORY_EMBEDDER_BASE_URL="https://dashscope.aliyuncs.com/compatible-mode/v1" export MEMORY_EMBEDDER_MODEL="text-embedding-v3" export MEMORY_EMBEDDING_DIMS=1024 ``` Or use the OpenAI defaults with a single key: ```bash export OPENAI_API_KEY="sk-your-key" ``` See the [Environment Variable Reference](docs/env_reference.md) for the full list. ### 3. Chat Memory ```python from hy_memory import HyMemoryClient client = HyMemoryClient(mode="pro") # Write: plain text or OpenAI-format messages client.add("I love sci-fi movies, especially Interstellar", user_id="user_1") client.add([ {"role": "user", "content": "Recommend a movie"}, {"role": "assistant", "content": "Try Interstellar — a sci-fi masterpiece by Nolan"}, ], user_id="user_1") # Search: returns the profile / normal / proactive channels results = client.search("What movies does the user like?", user_ids=["user_1"], limit=10) for mem in results["memories"]["normal"]: print(f" [{mem['score']:.2f}] {mem['content']}") client.close() ``` ### 4. Working & Coding Memory Writes must include a tool-call trace (`tool_calls` or `role="tool"` messages) and take effect in `pro` / `ultra` mode only (`lite` ignores `scene` and stores everything as raw memory): ```python messages = [ {"role": "user", "content": "Fix the timeout in the search client."}, {"role": "assistant", "content": "", "tool_calls": [{ "id": "call_1", "type": "function", "function": {"name": "apply_patch", "arguments": '{"path":"src/search.py"}'}, }]}, {"role": "tool", "tool_call_id": "call_1", "name": "apply_patch", "content": "Patch applied successfully"}, ] client.add( messages, scene="coding", # or "working" user_id="user_123", workspace_id="github.com/example/service", # optional: isolate by repository / project branch="fix/search-timeout", # optional: requires workspace_id ) result = client.search( "Which timeout implementation was finally kept?", scene="coding", user_ids=["user_123"], workspace_id="github.com/example/service", branch="fix/search-timeout", limit=5, ) result["facts"] # fact layer result["experiences"] # experience layer result["chain_block"] # coding only: version-evolution context ``` ### 5. Routing, Source Isolation & Advanced APIs - **Automatic scene routing**: When `scene` is omitted, writes without tool calls go straight to `chat` (zero LLM calls), and writes with tool calls are classified once into `chat` / `working` / `coding`. For searches, `search_mode="default"` goes to `chat` with zero LLM calls, while `search_mode="agentic"` performs scene classification, query rewriting, and time-range parsing. See [Working/Coding Scenes](docs/scene_coding_usage.md). - **Separate memories by source**: Pass `source="openclaw" | "cursor" | "codex"` on `add()` and filter with `include_sources` / `exclude_sources` on `search()` to isolate caller applications independently of `agent_id`. - **CRUD & System 2 evolution**: `client.get(id)`, `client.update(id, text)`, `client.delete(id)`, `client.list_memories(user_id=...)`, and `client.evolve(user_id=...)` (triggers System 2 in `ultra` mode). - **Per-call embedding endpoint override**: Pass `embed_override={"base_url": ..., "api_key": ...}` to `add()` / `search()` or use `with embed_endpoint_override(...):` for concurrency-safe endpoint switching. For provider configuration, storage backends, scenes, and the complete API, see the [Usage Guide](docs/usage.md). --- ## System Architecture
Hy Memory provides three memory scenes (`scene`), one per kind of task. `add()` / `search()` go through the scene router first, then into the Chat or the Working / Coding pipeline (orange parts in the diagram are coding-only; without them the pipeline is Working): | `scene` | Tasks | Memory shape | |---|---|---| | `chat` | Small talk, personal information, preferences, general Q&A | Hierarchical memory (L0–L7) | | `working` | Productivity work: documents, spreadsheets, research, financial analysis, content creation, computer operation | Two-layer memory: session facts + reusable experiences | | `coding` | Software engineering: coding, debugging, testing, builds, APIs/SDKs, scripts, SQL | The same two-layer memory as `working`, plus a code version-evolution chain (diff chain) | ### 1. Chat: Memory Hierarchy For long-term personal memory. Raw conversations are abstracted layer by layer into facts, summaries, a profile, and higher-level cognitive structures: | Layer | Name | Content | |---|---|---| | L0 | `BASIC_INFO` | Basic information | | L1 | `RAW` | Raw conversation (append-only) | | L2 | `FACT` | Atomic facts (versioned, immutable records) | | L3 | `SUMMARY` | Session summaries | | L4 | `IDENTITY` | Reserved | | L5 | `KNOWLEDGE` | Reserved | | L6 | `SCHEMA` | Mental models (abstract narrative templates, graph layer) | | L7 | `INTENTION` | Prospective intentions (with an expiry; demoted to ordinary facts once expired) | **Modes** | Mode | What it does | Graph DB | Use case | |------|--------------|----------|----------| | `lite` | Raw-only embedding writes and searches, no LLM calls; `scene` and `layers` are ignored | No | Vanilla vector RAG, fast ingestion, zero LLM cost | | `pro` | + LLM extraction + reconcile | Optional (`MEMORY_ENABLE_GRAPH`, off by default) | Standard workloads | | `ultra` | + System 2 schema induction + cross-domain sweeper (triggered by `evolve()`) | Yes (always on) | Full cognitive architecture | ### 2. Working: Two-Layer Productivity Memory For getting things done. One session with tool calls (a trace) produces both layers at once: | Layer | What it records | Per session | Structure | |---|---|---|---| | **Facts** (`WorkingFact`) | What this session did: the task, the approach, the result | Exactly 1, no threshold | `statement`, `subject`, `files`, `details` (verbatim source) | | **Experiences** | Approaches that can be reused next time a similar task comes up | 0–N, must pass a value threshold | `task`, `search_keys`, `solution`, `boundary_envs`, `confidence` | The fact layer guarantees that work which was done is remembered; the experience layer makes what was learned reusable. The two layers link to each other (`fact.derived_experience_ids` ↔ `experience.source_fact_ids`), and superseded facts stay traceable through a task-progress chain (`fact_chain_summary`). ### 3. Coding: Two-Layer Memory + Version-Evolution Chain Coding **reuses the same two-layer pipeline and data schema** as Working. It differs in three ways: | | Working | Coding | |---|---|---| | **Extraction spec** | Productivity-task spec | Software-engineering spec: the subject must be code or a decision; record exact coordinates (file / function / branch) instead of pasting code | | **Storage** | `coding_memory.db` + `*_coding_keys` / `*_working_facts` collections | `coding_memory_cv.db` + `*_cv` collections, fully isolated from working | | **Version-evolution chain** | None | **Yes**: how many times the same code was changed, and what each change was | **Why a version-evolution chain**: fact extraction deliberately avoids pasting code (the budget goes to more informative coordinates), so a version that was later reverted never appears in a fact. That version is usually not in the working tree or at HEAD either, so it cannot be read back afterwards. The chain stores the real diff of every version with zero LLM calls, filling in exactly the information a summary inevitably drops. **Design highlights** (`hy_memory/coding/chain_store.py`): - **A decorator, not a retriever**: the vector layer decides which facts are returned; the chain only attaches, under each fact, every revision of the code it touches (the user's words for that revision + the real diff). - **Change sources**: local Git diffs (set `MEMORY_CODING_CHAIN_REPO_ROOT`), or deterministic replace actions with `path` / `old` / `new` in the tool trace. - **Chain granularity & isolation**: one thread corresponds to one block of one function in one file on one branch, isolated by `user_id` + `workspace_id`. --- ## Support ### Storage Backends - Vector stores: ChromaDB (default), Qdrant, FAISS - Graph stores (ultra mode): Kuzu (default), Neo4j - Working / Coding metadata: local SQLite ### Documentation - [Usage guide](docs/usage.md) — full configuration reference, API details, deployment modes - [Environment variables](docs/env_reference.md) — settings and defaults - [Search and Reader guide](docs/hy_memory_search_skill.md) — reader selection, schema quotas, rerank, and return channels - [Working/Coding Scenes](docs/scene_coding_usage.md) — productivity-memory routing, response shapes, and coding chain behavior - [Graph memory design](docs/pro_graph_design.md) — graph projection, rerank, relation paths, and deployment limits - [Environment template](.env.example) — a copy-ready configuration template - [MemHub README](memhub/README.md) — local-first desktop & CLI product overview, runtime commands, and privacy boundaries - [OpenClaw plugin](plugins/openclaw/README.md) — agent integrations live under `plugins/` (overview: [plugins/README.md](plugins/README.md)) ### License Hy-Memory is licensed under Apache-2.0.
